claims.text: Low hardness and strength in equimolar CoCrFeNiTi are primarily governed by unimpeded dislocation motion.
Equimolar CoCrFeNiTi has a highly homogeneous simple solid-solution microstructure with minimal lattice distortion.
The as-cast CoCrFeNiTi structure, whether FCC or BCC, provides few obstacles to dislocation glide and forest hardening.
The scarcity of dislocation obstacles produces excellent plasticity and machinability but only moderate strength.
Casting equimolar or near-equimolar CoCrFeNiTi can produce a single-phase solid solution with minimal second-phase formation.
Cold rolling followed by controlled aging or annealing can induce secondary precipitates or increase lattice distortion in CoCrFeNiTi.
Induced precipitates or increased lattice distortion act as barriers to dislocation motion.
The comparison is to be performed at room temperature and a quasi-static strain rate of approximately 10^-3 s^-1 in an inert atmosphere.
A homogeneous single-phase solid solution with minimal lattice distortion permits easy dislocation glide.
The absence of precipitates, severe lattice distortion, and complex twin networks facilitates dislocation nucleation and glide.
Easy dislocation nucleation and glide lower internal resistance during plastic deformation.
Low internal resistance causes low yield strength and hardness despite high ductility.
The as-cast single-phase alloy will exhibit low hardness and yield strength with high ductility.
The treated alloy will exhibit greater hardness and yield strength than the as-cast alloy.
The predicted strengthening of the treated alloy results from enhanced dislocation impediment and forest hardening.
The hypothesis is limited to near-equimolar CoCrFeNiTi simple solid solutions without secondary-phase contributions under room-temperature, low-strain-rate deformation.
Twinning or phase transformations may contribute significantly at other strain rates or temperatures.
Frequent deformation twinning or phase transformation in the as-cast state would falsify the proposed dominance of easy dislocation glide if those mechanisms contribute significantly to deformation.
Failure of an obstacle-containing treated alloy to show a marked hardness increase would falsify the proposed mechanism.
